module

public import Mathlib.Combinatorics.Young.YoungDiagram
public import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Basic

@[expose] public section

open YoungDiagram

def YoungDiagram.Cell (μ : YoungDiagram) : Type := μ.cells

instance (μ : YoungDiagram) : Fintype μ.Cell :=
  inferInstanceAs (Fintype μ.cells)

instance (μ : YoungDiagram) : DecidableEq μ.Cell :=
  inferInstanceAs (DecidableEq μ.cells)

/-- The simple graph of a Young diagram: two distinct cells are
  adjacent iff they lie in the same row or in the same column. -/
def YoungDiagram.toSimpleGraph (μ : YoungDiagram) : SimpleGraph μ.Cell :=
  .fromRel fun a b => a.val.fst = b.val.fst ∨ a.val.snd = b.val.snd

reformulations.difference: The Lean use site asserts CDS-colorability for every Young-diagram graph, using a single coloring whose first k color classes attain the maximum union size for every k. The paper initially states a characterization of all achievable tableau types by dominance of the chromatic difference sequence.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The graph is exactly the paper's partition graph (Definition 2), so its proper colorings are Latin tableaux. On the finite cell type, indepNumK is an attained maximum; allowing overlapping independent sets does not change it, since the sets can be disjointized without changing their union. The prefix equalities give color-class sizes δ₁, δ₂, … by successive differences. Proposition 3 says this sequence is weakly decreasing, so these equalities are equivalent, after relabeling colors, to the paper's sorted-color-class definition of CDS-colorability. Proposition 5 and Corollary 6 establish that existence of a tableau of type δ implies existence of every dominated type; the converse follows by taking type δ. The paper explicitly states this equivalence on page 4. The extra k = 0 equation is 0 = 0, and the empty diagram satisfies CDS-colorability; both boundary facts were proved in the scratch file.
